utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, my name is Joanne Richardson. On behalf of the Prosecution, good morning to members of the Defence team and good morning to Your Honours. Your Honour, I will be joined shortly by Mr. Di Fazio as well as Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Vasvija Vidovic, representing, together with Mr. John Jones, Mr. Oric. And we have our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, with us as well as our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I neglected to introduce -- as well I'm joined by our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, thank you and good morning to you too. So any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing and this is in the wake of a note or a copy of a memorandum that I received -- I found on my desk this morning. And it's a memorandum from the Defence to the CLSS asking for the verification of the taped record and a corresponding correction in two places relating to the testimony of the last witness on Monday, 29th August. Please whoever is responsible give this matter due attention and please make sure that the Trial Chamber is informed promptly, as soon as the corrections have been effected and the manner in which they have been effected, particularly the last correction. I remember it was one of the things that I had in mind when the witness -- when I saw the transcript. It is definitely the opposite of what the witness said. So let's proceed. Let's bring the witness in. Do you plan to take the whole morning on -- the whole did -- I mean do you -- in other words do you think you will finish with this witness this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll certainly finish today. I might finish a bit before the end of the day, two and a half, three hours, estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. This is why I'm asking you any way. Ms. Richardson, if we finish early do you intend to start your cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I intended to start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Should be an easy witness, without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Kolenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Before I proceed any further, I want to make sure that you are receiving in your own language interpretation of what I am saying in English. All right. If you have problems with the volume and you want it to be adjusted, tell us and we will do it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if at any time during the course of your testimony here, you have problems with receiving interpretation, in other words, either it's not reaching you or you are not happy with the volume, please let us know straight away and we will make the necessary adjustment. So welcome once more. You are -- you have been summoned by the Defence in this case against Naser Oric to give evidence here, testimony. And very soon you will be sitting down and start answering the questions that will be put to you. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in several national domestic jurisdictions to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The next is contained in a piece of paper which the gentleman, our usher, is going to hand to you now. Please take that text in your hand and read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Please hand it back to the usher. Please make yourself comfortable. The important thing -- yes exactly -- that the microphones are near enough. So let me explain very briefly what's going to happen. I want you to remain calm and feel at ease throughout the whole of this exercise. It won't take long. Today, you will be asked questions by Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel in the Defence of Mr. Oric, whom you've met already, Mr. Jones. And then we will adjourn until tomorrow and tomorrow you will be asked questions by Ms. Richardson, who is one of the lawyers dealing with the Prosecution. What I would like you to do is to make sure that your answers are as short as possible but also that they are as precise as possible. Please don't try to give more information than you are asked. In other words, please try to answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. That will ensure that you will be back home this weekend. In other words, we plan to finish with your testimony tomorrow, which is Thursday, and after that I'm sure that arrangements would have already been made to facilitate your return back home. Last thing I want to tell you is that you will be -- the fact that you are being produced as a witness by the Defence does not entitle you to think that you are here to testify in favour of the accused. You are here to testify the truth. So please answer all the questions that are put to you. And don't try to distinguish between questions coming from the Defence and questions coming from the Prosecution. Your responsibility in terms of your solemn declaration is to answer every question irrespective of who is putting it to you, truthfully. All right? Did I make myself understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So welcome. We are soon going to start, and if at any time you need a break or anything like that or you're feeling tired, please let us know. My name is Carmel Agius, I am the presiding Judge. To my right I have Judge Hendrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark. To my left I should normally have Judge Eser from Germany but due to some urgent personal matters, he cannot be with us today and, in fact, we are sitting today, continuing to sit, pursuant to Rule 15 bis(A). And we will continue to sit like that also tomorrow. And then hopefully next week, the situation will change, hopefully to the better. So Mr. Jones she is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning from me, firstly, Ms. Kolenovic.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you start by giving the Court your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I am Sabra Kolenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And if you could confirm for us, please, the following details you were born on the 13th of June, 1958 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your maiden name is Gluhic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were married to Ramiz Kolenovic with whom you have two sons, Amel and Elvis?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Amel was born on the 21st of March, 1980?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was Amel born, please?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: In 1980, Amel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Elvis, when was he born?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of June, 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it right that you're the secretary of the association the women of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the correct name is the Association of the Mothers of the Enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. And finally, can you confirm that you graduated from the economic high school, I think it's called, in 1978?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then from 1978 you worked for an accounting service in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were born in Srebrenica. Have you lived in Srebrenica all your life?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What was your address where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Marsala Tita street.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the current name of that street in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Today the name of the street is Karadzicava, after Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours we have a set of photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm proposing to tender them as one exhibit the ten photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Not the ones we have here in our --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes the same ones I think it might be more convenient to have one exhibit number and I might even for the sake of convenience, provided there had is no objection, ask for an exhibit number now for these ten photographs and then I can go through them. They are numbered on the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would only inquire as to the source of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What will be the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D725, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, this will be D725.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, you'll see some photographs which are being put in front of you. Did you provide those photographs to us?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did they come to be in your possession?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th anniversary of the fall of Srebrenica and since the genocide, we were given these photographs, some people, some foreigners brought them to our office, I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know when they were taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can start with the first photograph and, as I say they, are numbered on the reverse side, I'm going to ask if you could look at that photograph on the ELMO and firstly tell us if you recognise the street there?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me, but can I just take my glasses from my bag?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, while she is doing that, let's -- they may be marked on the back, the ones that she has but the ones I have are not. So if perhaps you would show me the photo from -- oh, I see, all right. Okay. All right. Okay. It's the small handwritten number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, top right corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are talking of photo number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, this is photo number 1 in the series.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you have your glasses with you now, Ms. Kolenovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recognise this street?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's my street and the building where I lived until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm not sure if it's on the ELMO but if it could be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was yes, it is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you Ms. Kolenovic just point to where -- well, firstly do you see your apartment on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not all of it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you please point to it with the pointer you're being handed?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: That's the balcony of my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you want her to mark the photo or not? Or will you be using them with others?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I may or may not be using it with others but I don't think it's necessary for her to mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but for the record, the witness has pointed to the open veranda on the right-hand corner of the photo, which is the highest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Since we can't see all of your apartment there, can you tell us what floor it was on and whether it was on the top floor or whether there were floors above it?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the top floor, the sixth floor, and there were no other apartments above. There was just a flat roof above.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you mentioned that your apartment had a terrace. What sort of a view do you have from the terrace?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I could see the bus station from my balcony, as well as the neighbouring buildings. I could also see in the direction of the secondary and the elementary schools so I had a view of the whole town from the balcony of the children's room. That used to be the children's room. It used to be the bedroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you also see the hospital and the PTT building or not?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that your apartment was on the top floor. Were you able to access the roof of the apartment building from your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was using a storage space or a room up on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of view did you have from there of the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I had a better view than the one from the terrace and the room, once I got up on the roof. I could see a wider area and I could see what was going on in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to take you to 1992. Were you living in this apartment in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a number of inhabitants of Srebrenica left the town in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: This was in April, mid-April. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what caused people to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: You could sense it beforehand. There were stories going around already in 1991 when the war started in Croatia. Some Serbs came and they talked about the war there, how they were leaving. I never believed it. The only time I believed it was when I was watching television and could see a building being destroyed in Croatia and the balcony was hanging off and I was just wondering what kind of a force was it that could damage a building in that way and make the balcony hang like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When inhabitants left Srebrenica in April, mid-April 1992, were many educated or qualified people left in the town? Among the Muslims, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Practically none. The only people who remained were people with a secondary school education. All the intellectuals had left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's not in dispute, I take it, that in April 1992, Srebrenica was taken over by the Serbs. Were you in Srebrenica when it was taken over?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What, if anything, signalled to you that the takeover of the town had taken place? Did you see anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb families, the women and children, were the first to leave Srebrenica. After them, the Muslims from Srebrenica started to leave, and the news spread very quickly that they had gone to negotiations in Bratunac. Dr. Sabih Sehomerovic -- and when they came back, they said that they couldn't reach any kind of agreement with the Serbs and they left Srebrenica. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then did you actually see anything which signalled to you that the Serbs had actually taken over Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can, I think, Mr. Di Fazio and Ms. Richardson, he can lead on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not something that is in dispute, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you at some point see a procession of Serbs going through Srebrenica with a flag indicating that the town had actually been taken over?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone in that procession?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who? Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Zekic. I recognised him. His nickname was Zmiro, Milisav Gavric. I recognised many other of my neighbours. I don't want to mention all of their names. Perhaps I'll make a mistake with the last name. There were also people from other places whom I knew from the Bratunac municipality. There were people from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for Goran Zekic, was he armed or unarmed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, he was armed or he was unarmed?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when Srebrenica was taken over by the Serbs, did you continue to live in your apartment or did you go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, you have to say whether you continued to live in your apartment or whether you went somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I continued to live in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were your sons with you in that period?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how about your husband?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: My husband left to the Petrica street where my family used to live, and he went to see how my parents and the rest of my family were and he never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Are you saying he never came back, you never saw him again, or he didn't come back for a particular period of time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He did not come back over a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when, in fact -- where in fact did your parents and the rest of your family and your husband go during that period, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know roughly whether they went to the woods or whether they went to other houses or some other location?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Upon my husband's return, well, then I could talk about it, but for the whole period that they were away, I did not know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So you later found out where your husband and your relatives had been. And where had they been?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the neighbouring forests, behind every street, behind every house. In the Petrica street there is a forest, so they were hiding in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, sticking with you and your apartment, how long roughly were you and your sons in your apartment before the Serbs left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: More than 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why didn't you escape to the woods?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was unable to. I would certainly have fled had I been able to but whenever I tried to get out, my neighbour, Bosko Oric, prevented me from leaving the apartment building. He always sent me back to my flat and he said, "Close the shutters and don't look out of the window."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you in fact at any stage during this 20-day period look out and see what was happening in the town?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, was this neighbour a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was stopping her from --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kolenovic you heard the question, if you could answer His Honour's question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosko Oric, or whatever his name is that used to stop you. He used to send you back to your apartment. Was he a Serb or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were telling us that you did actually see some at least of what happened in the town of Srebrenica during this 20 days that you were in your apartment. Can you just explain briefly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you -- what I mean by that, apologies if I wasn't clear -- explain if you saw any activities of the Serbs in Srebrenica, if you saw what they were doing, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Can you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. During this period that you were in your apartment, you've told us that you at some stage at least looked out over the town and you could see the town. Did you see anything unusual in was there anything which struck you when you looked out over the town?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On a daily basis, for a number of days, close to my apartment building in Bato's house, there would be people arriving from everywhere. Our locals, our neighbours, I mean from Bratunac, Kravica, Skelani, because I heard them shout, "the Skelani people have arrived," "the Kravica have arrived," "the people from Sase have arrived," et cetera. That's where they gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, during -- you told us how you and your sons were in your apartment during the Serb takeover of the town. Did any Serbs ever come into your flat? By that I mean actually entering your flat during that period.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what happened on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I asked for help on a number of occasions, I asked Bosko Oric to at least allow me to go into the woods somewhere and he never allowed me. He always swore at me or used bad language, and he used to warn me that I was not to leave the flat at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And leaving Bosko aside, did anyone else, any other Serbs, ever come into our apartment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 12 people from Skelani did come and they broke into the apartment. They broke the door by kicking the door, and the door had been locked but it just was broken and my sons were with me in my flat and they asked me where Bosko's weapon was, who was -- there was a person who was from Skelani who used to live on the fifth floor and I said that I did not know who had what in their flats and why they were asking me about it. And following that answer from me, he hit my son Amel. When he hit Amel I tried to protect my child and then he started hitting Elvis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll give you a moment to recover your composure, if you can. Are you all right to continue, Ms. Kolenovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm taking over for a while, Mr. Jones. Madam Kolenovic, do you want a short break? Because I don't like this, let's have a short break. We will be outside. As soon as -- the important thing is I don't want any cameras on at this moment from now on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just have a Kleenex, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, they are over there. Help her, usher, please. Let's break for a few minutes. When you think we can continue, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll indicate it to Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are waiting outside but we will wait as long as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones. I certainly don't want you to misunderstand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I anticipate what Your Honour might say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are anticipating, so I won't in -- I will leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. If I might just say that there is a direct and specific relevance of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not contesting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, of the sons, of the treatment of the sons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I was literally trying to be extremely careful the way I put it because I see the relevance, too. I'm not saying that there's no relevance --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- but if we can avoid as much as possible putting the witness in a position where we will have a repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I rely on you. I think you have enough experience to deal with this. I don't think you need any lectures from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I propose to do Ms. Kolenovic is -- I'm not going to stick with this subject we were discussing any more at present. I don't want to upset you. I may need to come back to it later on but for the moment we are going to move to another subject area altogether, if that's clear. Right. Now, you've told us how during the Serb takeover of Srebrenica, you were in your apartment for about 20 days. Did you emerge at some point and actually leave your apartment and go into the streets?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say no, are you referring to the 20 days that you were in Srebrenica or are you saying you never -- I take it you're not saying you never left your apartment. What I'm interested in is, after the 20 days, did you leave your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you left your apartment and went out into Srebrenica, was -- did the town appear -- did the town appear to you as it was before this 20 day period when you were in your apartment or was it different in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can go direct on this, unless I hear an objection from Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it this way, Ms. Kolenovic: Did you see evidence that houses had been burnt when you left -- when you went out into the streets of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise, but I would prefer you to first of all get done with this matter of my sons, and not talk about how I left or did not leave after they entered my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you're okay, if you're in a fit state to finish talking about what happened to your sons during this 20 day period, then please do tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Madam Kolenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they entered my apartment, the people who entered were from Skelani and they asked me about the weapon and where it was that supposedly belonged to - and I've mentioned his name before, the neighbour who used to live on the fifth floor - and I said I did not know what stuff anyone had in their apartments, and the guy said that there was a weapon downstairs and I reiterated my answer, and I said I didn't know anything about it. And then he started hitting my son Elvis and he hit Amel and he pulled some of his hair out and he actually started bleeding, it was so rough, and I tried to protect my children. I was unable to help them. And then they beat me up as well. They kicked me and they used rifles and they took turns, and when we were lying on the ground, they were jumping on us and they beat us all up, all three of us, and then they left the apartment and we were still lying in the corridor and something could be heard from downstairs, the fifth floor. They were ransacking the apartment presumably, and after a few minutes they came back to our floor. We did not move. And one of them was holding a rifle. This was the first time I had set my eyes upon this rifle that they called "the sniper," and I will never be able to forget it as long as I live. And he threw the rifle in the air and then he caught it again and then he said to me, you are Balinkura. Thanks to this rifle, you and your children stayed alive. Had we not found the rifle we would have slaughtered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned this word Balinkura. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know someone called Ciro Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he ever come to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic I don't want to ask you anything more about your sons if it's going to upset you. So please let me know whether it's okay to move to this subject otherwise I'll move to a different subject. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I can talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just explain what Ciro, what, if anything, Ciro Jovanovic did when he came to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Ciro Jovanovic asked where my son-in-law was because my brother-in-law supposedly was -- because they were best friends. My brother-in-law's name was Safet Suljanovic and he asked me where he was and I said I didn't know. I said he had left Srebrenica and I didn't know about his whereabouts and I didn't know where his family was either. And Ciro, from that day, for 20 days running, came and took my children and took them somewhere in town, I don't know where, but every morning when he came, I appealed to him, and I offered him to take all of my property, everything I had in my flat, and to spare my children but he would come to collect my children every day and in the morning when he came for the first time he said he was going to take them and I asked him just not to kill them because they were young children. Elvis was only 7 and Amel was only 12. On the day after, when he came again, he would just fire some bullets and they knew that they had to go downstairs, that it was him. And so as not to have too much time to talk about it and I mean it is very difficult for me to talk about my children. I find it extremely hard. Your Honours, I do apologise but I don't want to interrupt proceedings again, but this is something that is extremely difficult and it's something I can't talk about without breaking down and without crying, and in the evenings, when children came home, they were always exhausted and dirty and they had been beaten, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic I don't want you to be upset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest, Madam Kolenovic, I know this is important for you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise but I must say all this to you. I'm here because I want to tell you the truth, nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just try to answer because this is not an investigative procedure. This is -- you happen to be in a courtroom where there is one individual who is standing trial, and the evidence that the Defence requires is evidence that is related to their client's case. I know these are very tragic events, very sad events, and I hope to God that no one has to pass through these events again in life. However, please, and I'm appealing to Mr. Jones as well, let's try and concentrate on what is strictly relevant to Mr. Oric, without, of course, interfering with what is relevant because you know what is relevant more than we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am appealing to you, Madam Kolenovic, to understand that not every bit of information of what happened in Srebrenica during this time is important for this case. There are many events that happened that are important and there are many events that happened, some of them personal, that may not be that important. I know they may be very important for you, but they may be completely irrelevant or not that important for Mr. Oric. And who is standing trial here is not the Serbian people or Mr. Jovanovic or the other person from Skelani but Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question -- as you will see, the relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, of course. I mean, I'm not in any way interfering because --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will become clear that the trauma suffered by her son is directly relevant to the charges in Kravica. I won't say any more at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But, Ms. Kolenovic, I do want to move on because we do need to make progress. We've heard about mistreatment of your sons and I do need to ask you about houses burning in Srebrenica, briefly. When you were in your apartment, did you see any houses burning in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During the 20 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, during the 20-day period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During the 20 days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Where in the town were these houses burning? Were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: In the very centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I ask if the witness could be shown photograph number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise this street?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What street is it?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: The street of Reufa Selmanagica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. We see in this picture that evidently there are some houses which have suffered damage. Do you know when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: All that happened during the period of time that Serbs stayed in Srebrenica, in April, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you actually yourself ever -- after this 20-day period, did you see Reufa Selmanagica street?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you left your apartment after the 20 days, did you see Reufa Selmanagica street?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it in this state or was it in some other state?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was even worse than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just give us a brief indication of what parts of Srebrenica, to your knowledge, were burnt after the Serbs had occupied the town?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing you can see here is just a small part, some of the houses which had been burnt down but in the centre of town, all Muslim houses had been burnt down and all Muslim businesses as well. Next to the supermarket and that's not too far from the mosque - you can't see it from here - there used to be an apartment building there, a two-storey building with two entries and only Muslims lived there. That building was set on fire and the people inside were trapped in there. Esad "Sumar" Fazlic and his wife, they were burnt to death in that apartment building, and near to the supermarket, Redzip's house, was also burnt down, and he himself was also burnt to death. And then Jelkic -- I can't remember his first name, and his wife, who was -- and then also the director of the public utilities company and his wife, and then again, behind the supermarket, not far from the mosque, another house, and that's where somebody else was burnt to death. It was in the area called Hrid, behind the mosque. All this is in the centre of town. Whoever stayed in their houses, they were all torched, burnt alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned Petrica before in your testimony. Were any houses burnt in Petrica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some houses were burnt and they were at the end of that street more or less, and were close to the forest. My neighbour, Salko Jusic, his house was set on fire, and he tried to get out, and as he was coming out, he was killed on the stairs of his own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you actually see his body?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know an area called Crvena Rijeka in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were any houses burnt in that part of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The entire street was burnt in that area and the houses were burnt facing the Domavija hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in total, and in -- I'm asking on the basis of what you yourself saw, put it this way: How many houses in Srebrenica, private houses, were not burnt?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Very few. If I may, Your Honours, I would just like to clarify this. When I left my flat for the first time, and I went in the direction of Petrica, my elderly parents were there and the rest of my family was there, and any able-bodied men had fled to the forests, and I had never seen anything more horrific in my whole life. It was a ghost city. It was a horror city. And it looked like a total waste land, and as I went from my flat to my parents' place, it's about one kilometre away, I was frightened so much that I couldn't even walk straight. I kept turning around because I felt I was being stalked or something by this horror, by the sheer horror of the situation, and I just could not comprehend how anyone could have done anything like that. I'd never seen anything more horrific. I had never -- actually I didn't see or meet anyone except a couple of dogs, stray dogs, who were running around, and there was a lot of rubbish in the streets, papers, people's belongings, some vehicles had been set on fire. Others had just been damaged. The town looked worse than what we had seen in some horror films, and when I went in the direction of Petrici, there is a building called the miner's building there, and the doors were gaping open and I could see a woman and three small children in the corridor and actually I could see their dead bodies because they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move ahead from this period after the 20 days that you spent in your apartment, when you came out into Srebrenica again. Firstly, do you know why or when the Serbs left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was it, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I was in my apartment. It was in May, the beginning of May. I don't know exactly what date it was. I can't really give you an exact date but it was when Goran Zekic was killed. There was such a fuss about it in town and then they simply disappeared, and what I've told you before - just in order to avoid any confusion or misunderstandings, Your Honours - when Goran Zekic was killed, I went to Petrica and I saw the way the city was, and throughout that period I had been in my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, this is in May 1992. I'm going to move forward into the summer of 1992 and, again, I take it's not in dispute that there was -- that subsequently refugees came into Srebrenica and that precipitated a refugee crisis. Now -- so I'd simply ask you a few specific questions about your experience of refugees coming into Srebrenica. Firstly, do you know roughly which or how many municipalities people came from into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I do know because I'm involved in the search for missing persons so I know exactly that people came from nine different municipalities, and they were arriving gradually in the course of the summer, and it was mostly rural population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you know roughly - you spent your whole life in Srebrenica - how many of the original inhabitants of Srebrenica actually remained or who were still in Srebrenica in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: In town, well only 370 locals remained in town, because I myself did not know about that before the city had been deserted and they had all taken to the woods or gone to the surrounding locations and when the Serbs left Srebrenica, only 370 locals stayed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's out of a pre-war population of how many?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: In the city itself, there were 5.600 people in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Turning to the refugees, let's say by the end of the summer of 1992, roughly how many refugees would you estimate were in Srebrenica? It's not necessary to have an exact figure, but just roughly.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there was nobody there who could organise a consensus of any kind -- a census, sorry, of any kind, and they kept arriving and throughout 1992 and 1993, people kept arriving from all sorts of places, so perhaps 50.000, roughly speaking. Some estimates point out to 50, other 40.000, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. But then -- I take it, then, that in that period in 1992, there were thousands of people who you didn't know. Would that be correct? In Srebrenica, obviously.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I believe that the witness answered to -- with respect to the amount of refugees, it happened over a period of time. So I'm not sure that counsel should be asking if there were thousands of people that she knew in the summer of 1993. Perhaps we can get an approximate number for the summer, but I believe her testimony as to the 50.000 covers 1992 and 1993, so that we are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Jones, if you could address this, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I can approach it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Basically I think it would be even better for everyone if you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic -- Ms. Kolenovic, over here. Let's take, say June 1992 or July 1992. As you walked around the town of Srebrenica, did you see a lot of people you knew or did you see a lot of people who you didn't know? You could just explain how that was.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I saw mostly people I did not know and there were thousands of them. I've already mentioned that, in 1992, refugees kept arriving from all of Eastern Bosnia, nine municipalities in all, and people kept coming into town and into some of the outlying Muslim villages, in the vicinity of Srebrenica. And in 1993, people kept coming. Some people were also leaving to go to Zepa. Those were coming from Zepa. So in case I didn't make myself clear, I simply wanted to say I don't know exactly what the number of people was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you personally have any problems or difficulties with refugees who were coming into Srebrenica in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you just give us an idea of some of those problems?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: We were in our apartment, and all of a sudden, it was like floodgates breaking and the refugees starting -- getting into those two buildings, and they opened the doors to my apartment and I wasn't counting them but there were certainly more than 30 of them, and we were so scared that the four of us just huddled in a corner. My husband and my two children and myself, we just didn't know what was going on. We were scared. And they went into the rooms and the kitchen and the corridor, and they kept saying, this is ours. And they -- some of them had some bags, others didn't. And they spent several days in our apartment. And we were not allowed to tell them anything at all because they had been driven out of their homes and each and every one of them had something really bad, some terrible experience to tell us about, so my husband and I simply did not dare tell them and explain to them that it was our apartment, that they had to leave, that several of them perhaps could stay, that we were happy to help, and so it was a period that lasted for about five or six days where we tried to put it to them gently that it would be better for them to leave, that there are other vacant areas, and to get at least some of them to leave my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Why couldn't you have them ejected by calling on the police or local authorities if such existed?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: What police?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it from that that there was no police force that you were aware of at that time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, I've told you what the situation was like in Srebrenica, and nothing whatsoever existed there. No local authority or anything like that. That had existed before the war, but afterwards, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When did these refugees come into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: In April -- no, sorry, in May. It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the year, please, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And do you know where some of these people were from?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They told me. They were Roma from Orlica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was about to use a map but I see the time, although we did have a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We did have 17 minutes. Of course, that is not enough. I was going to suggest that we go on for the time being and, of course, we will have a proper break and have the break when Madam needs it, most actually. I think if we can proceed for a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you are moving to some other area or you require a break yourself, then we will have another break. I want to make sure that you can -- that the break that we have had does not disrupt your --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your programme of finishing with this witness, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm still confident I can finish today. So we have copies of a map. In fact, it's the same map that was used with Ms. Hotic but we have clean copies because that one was marked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally while we are at this -- what I have just said is subject to requirements from the technical equipe and the interpreters. If you think you require a break now, then we will have it now. It's up to you. We will be having a break in any case. So please let us know what your preference is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kolenovic, you'll be receiving a map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we going to give this a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this will be D726.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you could just look to your right, Ms. Kolenovic, and see if you can locate, first of all, Srebrenica on that map. We need to pull back a bit.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, there is no need to mark Srebrenica but if you can locate Orlica on that map, that would also be helpful. If you look to your right, actually, Ms. Kolenovic, if you use the map.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You see Srebrenica to the left, Drina to the right, and only if you know where Orlica is and can locate it. I'm assuming there won't be any great objections on this matter. Do you see where it's written, "Drina," in blue on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There you go, Drina. You see where the words are written, "Drina"? And then take -- there we go. In fact, I will ask you if you could circle Orlica, please, with a pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has pointed to the towns of Srebrenica, the town of Srebrenica, and the village of Orlica, which she has encircled on Defence Exhibit D726. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or is about to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but my glasses are not that good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could you also encircle, please, Srebrenica, for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kolenovic, if you could just take the pen and circle Srebrenica with a nice, round figure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you have conversations with these people from Orlica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did they tell you how they came to be in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how came they to be in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: All of them had their own particular story, that they had to leave, that there was shooting there, that some villages were burned, that it was actually then that I got information about what was going on in Bratunac, that many people there were separated, that families were divided. In my apartment, the people who came also, they were not complete families. Some of them were hiding in the woods, some stayed in the houses, so that families were separated and whole families did not reach Srebrenica. A grandmother came with two children while the mother and father were somewhere else, and they never found out -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions before the break. I want to ask you about the food situation in Srebrenica, and, again, I take it it's not in dispute that there was a crisis in 1992-93. But I would ask you if you could describe the appearance of your sons, firstly, in that period, if you can do so without getting too upset. Just briefly, how did they appear? Did they appear as they did before the war or what? I think this might have been a mistake in the interpretation. The appearance of your sons is what I'm asking about. The physical appearance, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in my apartment. There was a large supermarket in my building. At the beginning, when the Serbs came, they first looted the whole of Srebrenica, all of the food was taken away from Srebrenica. I didn't have any need in the apartment to have food stocks, to have a reserve because I was used to going to town and buying whatever I needed. Every day I would buy one or two loaves of bread. I would do that every day so I didn't have too much extra food in the beginning so that right away, we were hungry and as Srebrenica was looted. I described the state that the Serbs left Srebrenica in. All that they could take that was valuable, they took. What was left, they set on fire. My car in front of the building was also driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter of clarification, when you say "every day I would buy bread," you're speaking about before the war, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was -- during the war, what was the longest period that you and your sons went without any food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you rephrase the question? It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 -- 21 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is what has happened. She has not understood your question. Before the war, you were asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, sorry, I meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how it is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No I said during the war what was the longest period you and your sons went without food, and she replied 21 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that, finally?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1992, late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's -- I did have one more question because I think it's best to finish this theme and then have a break. Did your -- I'm going to lead. Did your sons ever get in fights with each other over food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on a day when they were very exhausted. I cannot explain to you how people behaved during that time. These were no longer people who could control themselves. There was such exhaustion because of the lack of food and people no longer behaved in a normal way. I myself didn't behave in a normal way. Neither did my children. My son Elvis was going from apartment house from apartment house, from house to house, looking for a way to save himself, to find a scrap of bread, if anybody had any bread, not white bread but wheat bread. He had luck and he received a morsal. I found out later what happened between my sons. And he told Amel how he ate that small piece of bread. Amel knocked him down on his back, stepped on his stomach, and he had to throw up, and then when he threw up, he hit him, he kicked him in the nose and Elvis came home. He was all bloodied and crying. Amel was with him. And then I asked them "What happened?" I wanted them to explain why Elvis was bloodied, and then Amel said that Elvis ate this little piece of bread and that he didn't want to give any to him and that he did that to Elvis because Elvis ate the bread. I couldn't believe at the time what was happening with my children, why Amel, who loved his brother so much, why he would do something like that to him. My son Amel, who was older, was behaving in a strange way because he too was hungry and I, as a mother, couldn't help them in any way. I couldn't influence my children in any way to encourage them, to imbue them with some hope that things will be better, because I felt the same way. I was hungry, and I couldn't look for anything. So I didn't really condemn them because of what happened. It was just not a normal situation any longer. People were losing their humanity. It was an extraordinary situation. I really am not able to explain it any better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would like to take the break at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will have a 25-minute break. That would not impede with your schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kolenovic, before the break, you were telling us this story about your sons' behaviour and you said they were acting, or at least Amel was acting abnormally at the time. At this time, late 1992, early 1993, I think you said it was, was it just your children who were acting abnormally or were there other people in Srebrenica acting abnormally?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My children behaved like that, and all the other people too, children, women, all of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at that time, and when I say that time, let's say December 1992, January 1993, was it uncommon to see people who looked emaciated, who looked like they hadn't eaten for a long time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had been deprived of food for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My question was, was that a common or an uncommon sight, to see people who looked like they had been deprived of food for a long time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For people who hadn't eaten for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you just describe how the people, people you saw in Srebrenica in December 1992, how they looked? Describe -- give some examples.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They looked quite strange. These were no longer ordinary, normal people. People behaved like hungry beasts, like hyenas. I behaved like that, too. My children did. Everybody did. I was most afraid when this happened in 1992, when these were really no longer normal people. People simply turned into animals, even those people whom I knew, they no longer greeted each other, no longer asked each other, "How are you? Where are you?" Nothing. They would simply pass by you. They would either be making noises like cows, they would be making noises like barking dogs or roosters. I was very, very afraid. In those days, I didn't even dare move out of my apartment because a large number of people were walking up and down the streets. They themselves didn't know where they were going. I would always stop my ears so that I wouldn't hear these awful noises. This period actually put me into a situation where I was even more disturbed and affected, and I was even more afraid about what was going on with these people. So I didn't dare leave my apartment or I didn't allow my children to go anywhere either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said people were making animal noises. Do you know why they were making animal noises?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did that because they were hungry. They were very hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was the physical appearance of these people who you describe making these noises and walking the streets?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: They no longer looked like people. They no longer looked the way they looked before, the way they looked a few months before that. Everybody was very thin, just skin and bone. Those people whom I knew, when I met them, I would turn away so that I wouldn't see them. My children were like that too. My sons were so thin that their skin even had become thin. They were just skin and bone. It seemed to me that my son was just half a metre, he was so skinny. I had 48 kilos then, and now I weigh 62. And you can imagine, I had 20 kilograms less than I do now, so you can imagine how I looked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret's correction "42 kilos, I weighed."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Also there might be a correction too. "My son was just a half a metre"? Did you refer to your son's neck when you were talking about his appearance?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was talking about the neck. I would like to ask the Defence to understand what I'm saying. I already said that his neck looked as if it was half a metre long, so please don't confuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all. I wouldn't want to do that. It was just to correct the transcript. Now, you've -- we've looked at some photographs today and you told us that was during demilitarisation. Was the situation, as far as people getting food, was that better or worse or the same during demilitarisation? Had anything changed?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: A little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were people getting more food during demilitarisation than they were during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'll lead on air drops. Were there air drops of food in early 1993, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The question is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. It may be put to you that some of the people in these photographs don't look so terrible, they don't look so thin. Do you have any explanation in light of what you've been telling us for why some of these people don't look incredibly thin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would object to the way this is not only a leading question, but this is certainly going into almost a description of the -- by Defence counsel himself and I think the question can be put to the witness in another manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's no big deal, actually. I don't see any harm in the way the question was put, but perhaps if you rephrase it, you'll meet Ms. Richardson halfway. And I would suggest that you first indicate the relevant photos to the witness, give her a chance to see them one after the other, and then you can ask whatever question you like. I don't see a harm, much harm, or any harm in the way you put it, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Technically Ms. Richardson is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's look at photograph 8. Yes. Now, Ms. Kolenovic, if you would look at that photograph, the people there, you've been describing the appearance of people in late 1992. Did they look like these people or did they look in better shape or worse shape, if you could give us some sort of comparison, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: They were worse looking. Your Honours, I would like to say something. During the time that food was dropped from the air, I and my children managed to get two lunch packets on two occasions. We really couldn't get better or put on weight because of that. Some people were more skilled in getting more food and going to other places to get food, but I myself and my children only had two lunch packets each on two occasions, and that was enough to live on for a day or two. But not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. longer. This is something that I wanted to clarify, both to the Defence and to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now before air drops started did you actually go outside Srebrenica to find food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I must have not timed my objection correctly but if counsel will be putting any more questions to the witness with respect to a series of these pictures, I would at least like counsel to establish when in 1993 it is alleged these photographs were taken. We are hearing that they were given to the witness and I'd like to at least determine whether or not we have a month in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we would have had that cleared in the first place, in the beginning of the sitting, will it been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, she said during demilitarisation and that's -- if the Prosecution considers that insufficient they can re-examine on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these pictures were given during or taken do you remember demilitarisation. I think those are two different questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All we know is these photos were given to her and we have no further indication as to when they were taken. I think I got that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, they were given to her during the -- it's all in the transcript. I don't know why the Prosecution is getting this wrong. It was given to her on the 10th anniversary of the fall of Srebrenica, which is obviously not during demilitarisation, and they were taken during demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's about it. That's all we know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just so that we are clear with respect to laying the proper foundation and so that the photographs are properly examined by Your Honours later on, is it the witness's testimony that she was told they were taken? How do we know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can -- let's put it -- you either put the question now or you leave it for Ms. Richardson to put on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll leave it to Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I have understood is that these photos were given to her or them, as explained by Mr. Jones earlier on, or and by the witness, and that they are photos that, allegedly at least, the indication is that they were taken pre-1995 and during therefore the demilitarisation, but that's the only indication that we have. I don't think there is an indication as to the month or week or date. MR. DI FAZIO: Unless I've got it wrong, I don't have the transcript in front of me. I distinctly recall, Your Honour, that Mr. Jones quite rightly asked the witness when they were taken and the witness said in 1993. Now, that's my recollection of the evidence. I don't know if it was January 1993 or June or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can check that but the impression that I got is -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- or November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that -- the impression that I have is that they were given to her and that they were taken during the -- after demilitarisation came into --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I certainly have will have a series of questions about these photographs during cross, so that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It couldn't be January 1993 because that's pre-demilitarisation and the Prosecution should know when demilitarisation started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And may I also say, just for my purposes, I could have a picture of a man from any period and say, "Did people look better or worse?" For my purposes it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you -- I asked a question a while back whether you ever went outside Srebrenica to search for food. Is that something you did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you mention some of the places which you went to, to find food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I went on several occasions to all of the places where I would go with the rest of the population. Thousands of us would go to these places every day to look for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term "torbari"?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I don't know -- somebody called us torbari but we all had bags, torba.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would that refer to civilians who went to get food at this period?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody went to look for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask in general terms based on your expeditions to get food, did you observe whether the torbari went into actions -- sorry, went into villages before actions began or during actions or after actions? Can you provide us with some comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are getting into an area now where it's certainly contested issues, and I would ask counsel not to lead and have the witness -- put non-leading questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I take it that wasn't a suggestion that that question was leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't take it as leading but in other words, you're being put on the alert that there will be objections if you put leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, that was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it because otherwise the question is perfectly legitimate. I would split it because I think it contains too much in one sentence, but that's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, did torbari go in search of food purely on their own or were they sometimes searching for food in the course of an action?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: They would go on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to revisit that theme but I want to go to somewhere specific. Do you know a place called Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever go there or try to go there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Tried to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that, if you could tell us the month and the year -- or the month?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: This was in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Do you know the month when it occurred? Or sorry, when you went there?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it was September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're sure of the month? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the month. Your Honours, I just wanted to clarify, there is no place around Srebrenica where Muslim or Serb villages were, that the population did not go to in search of food. Before the war, I never left Srebrenica. I was not familiar with the villages around Srebrenica. But everything I went through in 1992 and there were some terrible things, all of that is mixed up for me now. I don't know which month. I don't know the dates. Even now I still don't know my son's name, well, thank God that I'm still normal enough to be able to speak with people in a normal way. So I would like you to take into account what I am saying, that we don't go into too many details when this was. I really did go to Fakovici with the other people. There were quite a few of us.
