There were thousands of us. And nobody counted these people. And nobody could ever say exactly how many people there were. Wherever we would go, there would always be thousands of us, not 1.000 but thousands of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that you tried to go to Fakovici. Do I understand that you didn't actually reach Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why -- why did you not actually reach Fakovici itself?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I got to one village, and that's where I heard the name of that village, but the shelling was very intense, and the shooting from Fakovici. People were coming back and some were passing by. Some were wounded or carrying the dead. There was shooting in all directions. Thousands of people were on the move. Some of them were going there, some were coming back. It was such a state of chaos that it's very difficult to describe. Why such numbers of people would be going in the direction of the shooting. But some people were going in that direction and some were returning from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What led to you being en route for Fakovici in the first place? Why were you trying to go there or how did you know to go there?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly like to ask the Defence counsel -- well, I didn't go anywhere just for no reason. I only went in search of food. I wasn't thinking about my own life. I wasn't thinking about the shelling. I didn't think that I might get killed or trip on a mine or that I wouldn't bring something back. All I had in front of me was that I would go there and bring something back for my children. So, please, if you can, don't ask me about that too much. I'm only here to tell the truth. And, Your Honours, I would like to ask you also to know that I am here out of my best intentions, and I'm only here to tell the truth. I never went anywhere other than to look for food. I did that as well as the rest of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kolenovic, there might have been a misunderstanding. I'm certainly not suggesting anything other than that you're here to tell the truth. That's plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut it short, I think if you don't mind, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to stop a little bit, Madam Kolenovic, or shall we continue? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just -- and we will close on this. How come that, out of all places you decided to go, and others decided to go to Fakovici? How come it was Fakovici and not somewhere else? This is what Mr. Jones tried to make you answer. Am I correct, Mr. Jones? Because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- if I'm not interpreting your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue it if the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, but if she can answer the question, she can answer it. If she can't answer the question, then we will move to something different, because Fakovici was quite a distance away. I mean, it's not getting out of Srebrenica and it's around the corner. It's quite a few kilometres away. So how come you -- the rest of you decided to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The entire population that originated from various municipalities around Srebrenica knew where Serb villages were, and they knew that it was the only source of food, and that was the only thing that we could do for our survival. So we went to all those Serb villages. I myself went to some Muslim villages as well, and I was forced to steal food. I would sneak into a garden and actually steal food to take back home to my children, and I used to do that in Muslim villages as well. I mean, I would have stolen stuff from my own father had I had to, to give to my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just have one further question on Fakovici. You said that people were coming back from Fakovici and there were wounded and some were carrying the dead, there was shooting in all directions. Did people say anything about the shooting, about where it was coming from?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: From the houses in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever go to the Bjelovac area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Sase in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was by the end, it was winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that before or after this -- before or after you went to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You went to Sase, then Fakovici. Did you return to Sase after Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I only went to Sase once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Can you -- can you describe what happened when you went to Sase?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I can. I set off like every other time, with other people. There were women, children, and whoever was able to walk. Some elderly women as well who were strong enough to walk. There were thousands and thousands of us. I can't tell you how many thousands. And wherever we went looking for food -- I mean, I can't really specify but we are talking about at least 20.000 people on the move. And I got to Sase and there was horrible shooting. I could hear it coming from Sase. And I paid no heed to that and the others didn't either. We were like hungry hyenas. We were so starved and we gathered up all our strength simply to get our hands on some food. The other refugees -- I mean, I myself was in a slightly better situation because I was in my own home and I had my own bed to sleep in and I had my own crockery, my own sheets, and all that, but there were people who were much worse off; the refugees, I mean, they had nothing at all. What was important to them was to get into a house, any house, no matter whether it was a Serb or a Muslim house, they needed to get their hands on some clothes, maybe get some pants, because they had no property at all. They couldn't even change their children's clothes. Now, I myself did not need any of that. All I needed was some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But if you could focus on Sase and -- firstly, you've told us how you would go looking for food. Did you find any food in Sase?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, when I entered Sase, I was surprised. I saw depots such as you wouldn't believe. Today, looking back, if I think of that, I simply can't help wondering how anyone managed to stay alive in Srebrenica since we saw so many casing and cartridges et cetera, and they had antiaircraft machine-guns and guns and those are these weapons that they called PAMs, and I kept wondering throughout the war how powerful a weapon it had to be, but when I got up to Sase I was really surprised to see how many lethal weapons must have been used. There were piles of these casings and cartridges, and it was only from that one single village that all of that had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And then in terms of food, did you find any food or did you see any refugees finding food? What happened in that respect, please?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a bit of a sad story, even though it might have a funny side as well. A pig came along from I don't know where. About 2.000 or 3.000 of us refugees basically chased that pig. And we were so exhausted because the pig was running around from one hill to another and it was just running to and fro until the pig itself was exhausted. And something else that I find simply unbelievable but that's what happened, was that people fell upon the pig and they actually killed it with their bare hands and they took the meat, there were hundreds of people clamouring for this meat and they dismembered the pig with their bare hands. And I myself got into the fray and tried to get my hands on anything I could, just a little bit of that pig, and people were walking all over me, they were jumping over me, and so I got hurt, in fact, and for a while I found it impossible to get up. And as I was lying on the ground, some left and there was snow all over but snow had melted and there was -- you could see the ground, and some blood on the ground as well. And some of those people, and there were children there, and they were licking the blood of the pig. I myself did not manage to find any food at Sase. I don't know how I can put this into words, how I can explain to you how those people behaved. I can't help wondering even now. I mean, how did they find it in themselves to actually dismember a pig with their bare hands?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that day that you were in Sase, do you know where your husband was?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He was with other people, fighters and civilians. I would have gone to Bjelovac to look for food as well but there was horrific shelling then and we could see dead and wounded, a lot of dead people who were being brought back and the wounded coming back so I didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was your husband among the wounded or was he -- was he not wounded on that day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When my husband came home, I found out that he had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know how he came to be wounded?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He was wounded by a shot from a house in Bjelovaci and a bullet went through his shoulder. So his bone is damaged, so this bit here. And I barely managed to get his shirt off because it was stuck because of dried blood, and you could see the bone as well. So his shirt and his vest were all soaked in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else of what had happened or what had been going on in Bjelovac that day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He told me everything. He told me that in Bjelovac, in every Serb house in Bjelovac, there was a lot of weaponry, and I had forgotten to say before, and so I'm going to say it now, that he himself brought back a rifle. I can't remember which one it was, because I don't really like to talk about arms, but I think it was an automatic rifle. And so he had found a rifle as well in one of the Serb houses, and he said that people were shooting at them from inside the houses, and he was wounded, as I said, in his shoulder, and he also said that there were lots of civilians, too many civilians, women and children, who were being killed and there were too many wounded, and the way he told the story to me was that there were hundreds and hundreds of them, and that all hell broke loose and there was a lot of noise, the screaming, the shooting, and they themselves didn't know what to do. They didn't know how to help. They didn't dare return the fire because there were too many civilians in their way. So they simply could not save them. They couldn't defend them. And he also told me that planes were dropping bombs on those civilians and that quite a few civilians, women and children, and men as well, and quite a few of them were wounded as a result of that air raid. And I myself saw, when I was in Sase, I saw a green plane, it was a green-coloured plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you mentioned planes dropping bombs on civilians, are you talking about Serb civilians, Muslim civilians, what precisely? And this is obviously what your husband told you.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about Muslim civilians here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One thing which you can perhaps help us with: You said in Sase that there was some snow but it had melted or something of that nature. Was there snow on the ground that day or not? What precisely was the situation?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: There was snow on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember - only help us if you do - when snow first fell in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Roughly, roughly when in the year, what month?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was November, December or January.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've described earlier being in Fakovici. Was there snow on the ground when you were in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about a place called Kravica. Are you familiar with Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you -- did you go to Kravica at some point to find food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you help us with when that was, the month and year?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you able to be more specific about the date or is that the most that you recall?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: The 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The 8th of which month?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: The 8th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you were in Kravica on the 8th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, obviously you were living in Srebrenica at the time. When did you leave Srebrenica to go to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, where you went on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I went together with all the other people, I can't remember how many exactly but several thousands, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember which -- which place you -- well, let me put it this way: Where did you spend the evening of the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, I said I'm not really familiar with the area but I think it was Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you actually stay in that place, if it was Jaglici, what sort of accommodation did you stay in? In a building or in the open air?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was only one house there and it was a mill.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you spent the night there and then you've told us that the next day you were in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, were you able to enter Kravica without any difficulty on the 8th of January? Or did you encounter any obstacles?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, you had difficulties entering Kravica or you were able to go in without any problem?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I could not enter Kravica, not just I myself but the rest of us. I don't know whether there were fighters but there were some people wearing civilian clothes, they were men. And they were preventing us from going into Kravica. They were telling us not to go and they even pointed their guns at us and they said we'll shoot you, turn back. But there was no possibility of stopping us from going. Nobody could stand in my way because my only intention was to get food. I focused on that only because that was the only source of food in Kravica because we knew that there were Serbs living there and we knew that that was the only last source of food that was still left and that was the only way we could ensure our survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, these people who tried to stop you, were they Muslims or Serbs, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims, of course, not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And they tried to turn you back, to stop you going, but I take it they didn't stop you or they weren't able to?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were trying. They were doing their best in order to try and stop us. They were threatening us, they were shooting into the air. Some of them even pointed their guns and rifles at us and they were swearing at us but there is no one who can stand in the way of a crowd, of a hungry, starved crowd of people. There is nothing that can stop that flood of people. The only thing we could have done would have been to start fighting amongst ourselves. I would have attacked even my own father, even whoever. I mean, I didn't allow anyone to stand in my way. All I could see in my mind's eye was food down there and nothing more. I mean, I do apologise for getting a bit emotional, but I don't know how to say it in any other way. But this is just to say that everything I could think of at that time was just food, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told us you went into Kravica on the 8th of January. At that time, was there any sign of any military activity or was it completely quiet?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: We could hear shooting, shelling. We could feel that it was coming from some areas but I can't tell you exactly. I can't specify where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you about your family members on that day. First of all, your husband, was he -- was he with you on the 7th of January or was he elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know where he was on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He was in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what he saw or observed on that day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What did he tell you, briefly?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: He criticised the civilians, in fact. He said why did they have to create so much chaos in Kravica? They entered and I myself would do that wherever I went looking for food. In order to frighten the Serbs and get them to leave their houses, let's say five or six or 10.000 of us would enter the village but I can guarantee that in Kravica, well, perhaps 5.000 could have gone to Kravica. The entire population of Srebrenica must have been in Kravica on that day. It is unspeakable. I mean, it's like some kind of film. People were crying, screaming, banging pots and pans. They were driven in a way which was totally frightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One point in the transcript. In English, and please, I'm correcting something in the English, I'm not questioning your answer. But it says in English, perhaps 5.000 could have gone to Kravica. Was that what you said, that it was about 5.000 people who went to Kravica? Or did you give a different figure?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I meant was that perhaps around 5.000 people had stayed behind and all the others went to Kravica. The entire population, only the ones who were sick and bed-ridden stayed behind and all the others went to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you about your sons. I'll start with Amel. Was Amel -- did you see Amel on the 7th or 8th of January or did he -- was he elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I saw him in Kravica. And I had left him behind at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. Jones. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned how your son was in Kravica with a group of boys, a large group of boys. At that time, this is January 1993, but I want your answer -- when you answer, to include late 1992 as well, if you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can. Was it common or uncommon in Srebrenica to see groups of children going around unsupervised?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it was common or it was uncommon?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was uncommon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Were there many -- or were there, to your knowledge, orphans in Srebrenica in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what -- during -- leaving aside Kravica for the moment, your sons, during the day, were you -- were you supervising them or were they left to their own devices?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: They were left to their own devices. Your Honours, if I may just say this, there was a child without parents staying with me at my apartment for about five or six months, until he found out where the rest of his family was. His parents were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, did you -- you've told us you were in Kravica on the 8th of January 1993. Now, and you've told us that your -- I'll withdraw that. Did you on the 8th of January 1993 see any houses which had been burnt or damaged by fire?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just saw a lot of smoke, smoke from shells. That's when there was a burning, there was fire in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. What time of day were you in Kravica on the 8th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Not early in the morning but it was in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know what part of Kravica you were in on that day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Somewhere near the school, not right next to the school but not far from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if the witness can be shown one of the photographs which is part of P400 and the ERN number is 01087912. It's just one of those photographs. In fact, if it assists, I can provide my own copy but it has writing on it, that's true. 7912.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kolenovic, if you could look at that photograph, firstly, and tell me whether you recognise what it depicts.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what does it show?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: That's the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 8th of January 1993, was it in the state that you see it in that photograph or was it in some other state?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It looked different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How different? In what way?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I see here that the school is damaged. Then, when I was there on the 8th, it didn't look like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Was it damaged when you saw it on the 8th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you -- after the 8th of January, did you ever go back to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really say how many days later, three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Three or four days later, so the 11th or 12th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why did you go to Kravica on that day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Because, again, we didn't have any food, and I definitely set out for Tuzla with the children. It was the only hope I had of getting out of the hell that I was in with the children. And I went with the intention of reaching the free territory, not thinking of where I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What time of day was that on the 11th or 12th of January? Was it morning, afternoon, evening?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: We left in the evening because we were expecting the Serbs to shell and to return to the hills around Kravica, that they were coming from the direction of Bratunac because that was their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were expecting Serbs to shell. Did you actually come across any shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you see where the shelling was coming from and where the shells were landing?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely. From the direction of Bratunac, behind the school, there is a hill, and there were loud detonations and shelling from behind that hill that was falling on that part of Kravica towards Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did that present any difficulties or danger to you at the time, to you and your sons? Or were you out of the way of the danger?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't thinking about the danger. I expected that. I just went with the intention of whatever, whether we would get killed or whether we managed to cross into free territory. I went towards death, and if we managed to survive, very well, but this wasn't something that surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So is it right that you didn't have to hide from shelling or take cover? You were able to just pass through Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So what is the truth, please?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: This is why I said that that's not true. An airplane of a green colour went -- it sensed, I don't know, I can't really say exactly how many there were, perhaps there were over 500 women and children, there were entire families there. There were also those who were wounded in this column that I went in with my children. And then suddenly, behind the hill, a plane appeared. It was green. And it was flying very low. So that I could see it when I looked up. First of all I could hear the sound. You kind of sense the sound that something is coming towards you and then the plane appeared behind the hill. The plane was open and it was so low that I could see two soldiers with -- because I know what a machine-gun is. I asked my husband about it during the war because at the beginning of the war, I saw when the Serbs entered Srebrenica that they were carrying these cartridge belts with bullets and I knew that these were machine-guns. They were carrying them. And they were shooting at us from these machine-guns, and they were flying very low and we were trying to flee. Some people, several people, were killed there. A woman was killed, her baby was wounded. And suddenly, this plane then disappeared. We ran into the houses and sought shelter there. The plane left. It went back behind the hill. And then we set off again. And then when we set off again, again we heard the sound of the airplane, and it was very close to us again immediately and it just dropped some kind of white powder and because of this white powder my son, Elvis, fainted. It wasn't -- this was an asphalt road, a street. There was no bridge or anything there, just some small crossing there. There is a creek there. We reached the creek. One young man took my son and put him in the water and then Elvis came to. And then we were crouching underneath that bridge when the plane went behind the hill again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when the plane flew over and was shooting at you on the ground, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: On the street. We were going straight through Kravica towards Konjevic Polje. We were going straight down the street. We didn't go over the hills or anywhere else. We were going straight down the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a question or two about Amel. You told us before, a story about how he fought with his younger brother and was behaving abnormally. Had he, in addition to that mental abnormality, did he suffer any physical injuries when he was in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what caused those injuries?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, they were mistreated on a daily basis, and beaten when Ciro was taking him and Elvis out every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us about that. I mean, aside from those incidents, was he injured in any other way?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Amel was, yes. In 1992, also, there were green planes flying over, and there was some apparatus on them, they looked like water heaters. They had nails and some things wrapped up. I don't even know how to describe that. It just looked like a water heater. And they were throwing those down. At that time, my Amel was at the playground and there were a lot of refugees there in the elementary and the secondary school, and sometimes Amel, for a moment -- well in 1992, from 1992 to 1993, I cannot remember whether there was one second at the time that the town was quiet and that there was no shooting, and he wasn't always able to be in the apartment or in some closed space or in the woods. So Amel went to the playground over there, and he was at the playground when they threw this kind of water heater thing from the plane, and one young man took him because of the bombing of the MiGs, the elementary school, the gymnasium had been damaged, there was no glass in the windows or anything, and then this young man took Amel and threw him on the first floor and that's when Amel was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I don't want to cut you off, but just so that we can make some progress. In sum, was Amel injured as a result of bombs or some water heater, rather, being dropped from airplanes on Srebrenica? Would that summarise what you told us?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was just about to say that Amel was wounded the second time. This is another time, when the MiGs were bombing Srebrenica. Amel was between the two detonations, these very heavy bombs. He was in between them and he was hurt quite seriously. He has 16 scars on his body because of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, and that was in 1992 you told us, by MiGs. Do you know, happen to know, have any information, where the MiGs were flying from?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: From Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, did Amel stay in Srebrenica until the fall of Srebrenica or did he leave before then?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Before the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I am exploring this because it does have relevance. Can you explain how he left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Once more we were hungry. The situation was becoming more and more tense. The first convoy that came -- I had terrible problems with Amel. He was under a lot of stress because of the bombing. He was in the hospital for three days. And he wouldn't speak at all. He would just look. Of course, I as a mother went through it quite well. Amel was always saying that he was going to jump from the sixth floor, that he really couldn't take it any more. And I had to tie him to my hand with a rope. He would always be jumping up and saying, planes, planes. Sometimes he would go down to the fourth floor, he would pull me behind him during the night, when he would say, "Planes, planes." He was stronger than I was. He would take me down from the sixth floor to the fourth floor, and I had to have so much strength and patience. I was already worn out trying to convince my child, who was suffering from trauma and from stress, I was always afraid that he would jump because he was always saying to me, "I'm going to jump. I'm going to kill myself. I can't stand this anymore."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did it actually come about that he left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: The first food convoy, when it arrived in Srebrenica, he told me himself, when this convoy arrived, "I'm going to escape, mom. I'm going to go somewhere. But, please, I'm asking you, let us go. We should leave." The whole population had come out to meet those four or five trucks, to try to get on and to try to save themselves. I was talking to my husband, and -- because we were both very worried about the children, and I decided that I had to at least get the children on to those trucks, if I managed to do that. In that war, sometimes they would say -- I apologise, Your Honours, if I can tell all of this. They used to talk about World War II and people throwing their children and I just thought about it and I was thinking, what kind of a parent would it be to be able to throw their child like that? But I myself, unfortunately, had to experience this in this dirty war. I was talking to my husband, it was sometime before dawn, it was still dark, the trucks were getting ready to leave Srebrenica, and almost the entire population wanted to get on to those four or five trucks. I don't know exactly how many of them there were. My husband asked some men to help them to throw the children on to the truck because the truck was overcrowded already, perhaps even 500 people had climbed onto the trucks. There were women and children there. Everybody was trying to grab on to the trucks. They were throwing them five or six times. They would throw them and then they would fall off again and then we would have to find the child and then this would happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to break this down a bit, firstly, when was this, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: This happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the month, roughly, if you're able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was perhaps in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've described the situation. Were the authorities, if there were such, controlling the situation or trying to control the situation, trying to stop people getting on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: What authorities are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So do I take it from that that there was nobody controlling the situation or trying to exercise control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the situation that was impossible to get under control. No one, absolutely no one, would have been able to do that. There was not a single person in Srebrenica who might have brought things under control. I've told you before, people acted in an extreme way. It was a fight for survival. That's what I did with my children as well. My husband could not stop me from doing what I wanted. I had problems with my own husband. He kept telling me, don't go, otherwise you'll get killed. And sometimes he asked us to leave. He said, "You go and save your lives and this doesn't matter what happens to me."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll withdraw what I was going to say, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just to finalise that topic, did your sons leave on those trucks and go to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They got their -- I found out after six months that they got to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear. Both of them, in other words, both your sons, both Amel and Elvis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm leaving your sons completely -- we finished discussing your sons. I want to move on to a completely different area and if you're able to continue, we will conclude shortly, in about five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we -- are you all right? Can we proceed? Or do you want another break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just have a couple of areas which I want to ask you about. You've described problems particularly for the refugees in getting hold of clothes. Now, did people ever actually make clothes themselves? Did they manufacture clothes in Srebrenica in 1992, early 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was in a slightly better position than the people who had been driven out of their houses. Those people who came as refugees only had the clothes they had on their backs. They couldn't last like that for three years. It wasn't really important for them to have a really comfortable bed to sleep on or whatever. All the couches, curtains, everything had been used in order to make clothes. Sometimes I found it both sad and ridiculous at the same time, if you could, for example, saw a man coming down the street wearing pink or flowered trousers, et cetera. So as I said it was extremely sad but ridiculous at the same time. They used whatever they could find in order to make clothes for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would that include sheets? Did people use sheets to make clothes?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that something you yourself saw?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. That was slightly more appropriate for making clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And did you see that yourself? Did you see people wearing clothes made from sheets?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, Your Honour, I'd like to clarify. In Srebrenica, there was a clothes factory, in fact, and a man who used to work there, I think he was the boss there, he managed to get out a number of sewing machines before the Serbs plundered everything and we had a fair amount of thread so it wasn't just a huge problem to make clothes. I mean some people did have problems but others didn't. So they would go and see him and ask him to give them that thread. Just so -- in order to clarify how come it was possible for us to get our hands on thread in such a situation. That's how we got it. And I myself was in a similar situation, sometimes. And I asked him to give me some thread and needles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You agreed you saw people wearing clothes made from sheets. Would these be coloured sheets or white sheets or black sheets? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on what they had. Some were white, others were multi-coloured. And I saw one man from Crvena Rijeka whom I knew. He said to me, I asked him, oh, you're wearing some new clothes. And he said, "This is made of a Duvet." And it was grey on one side and the other side was multi-coloured with some kinds of green flowers and leaves, a flowery pattern. So that's what he had on and he looked okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us how you were in Kravica on the 8th of January 1993. On that occasion, did you see among the people you saw anyone wearing clothes made from sheets?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What colours?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: White, multi-coloured. People used to make clothes out of traditional Muslim dress for women, those white trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I want to explore one more aspect of the use of materials. And only answer this if you can help us with this, but did you see firstly people who had been injured in Srebrenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to talk about it but I'm here to tell the truth, and that's what I should do. My flat was close to the hospital, and it would take me longer to descend the stairs from the sixth floor than to, you know, look in the direction of the hospital. All those who were wounded, women, children, the entire population, whoever was wounded, I couldn't help seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well I have a specific question in that regard. Was anything done to treat people who had blood -- blood flowing? Was there anything used to stop people from bleeding whether they were injured, if you saw that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband, whenever he went into action and when we all went somewhere together, he always had some bandages stuffed in his pockets, and I asked him why. And he said, "In case I get hurt." And he said, You silly woman, so as not to bleed to death." Even a small wound can be dangerous if it bleeds too much and so it is important to have a tight bandage so as to stop the bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if bandage is necessarily the best translation. Are we talking about a tourniquet, something used to stop bleeding?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were strips of cloth and I would cut them out for him using sheets or any other type of cloth. Well, once I had to rip up a flowery skirt of mine and I would sometimes give it to other people. Let me tell you once again I was in a somewhat better situation than the refugees who had to flee their homes with nothing but the clothes on their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And as far as you know, and only answer if you can, was it your husband alone who would go into action with bits of cloth to use as a tourniquet or did you see that being done by other men?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Others did that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Can I just -- sorry, do you wish to add something?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Even a slight wound could lead to death. There was nothing at all in Srebrenica. The hospital had been completely plundered in 1992. There wasn't a single tablet, let alone any other medical supplies or equipment. I was present when people's limbs were being amputated in a very rough fashion. People would tend to die even of a very small wound. So they had to somehow look out for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just two -- two last areas. Did you come across scabies or fleas or lice in 1992, late 1992, early 1993, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How common was it to find -- to come across people with scabies or fleas or lice? Was it common? Uncommon?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify this in the following fashion. We all had fleas in our apartments because, as you walk down the street, and then you came back and you took your clothes off and you shook them, everything was black. You were unable to walk down the street without bringing back fleas and whoever came to your apartment would leave at least ten fleas, and if you ever had even a single flea in your bed, it would be impossible to go to sleep. May I just add something else, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We used to be a civilised people before, but in the beginning of 1992, we were thrown back 500 years. I was a city dweller. I had all the amenities and then all of a sudden I found myself in a situation in which for a number of days I couldn't get any soap, any washing powder, any food, nothing, and imagine what it must have been like for those people who had already been wandering around the woods and forests for months. And they had nothing. They had no clothes, no shoes, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to clarify one last matter. Do you know what I'm referring to if I refer to scabies?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were there people in Srebrenica who had scabies in late 1992, early 1993, who you saw?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just describe what someone who was suffering from scabies, who you saw, what it did to their appearance, what they looked like, what it did to their physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: They were scratching themselves all the time and that led to scratches and wounds all over the body, all over the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a final subject. You've referred to demilitarisation so I'm going to ask you just about -- briefly about that period. Once there was demilitarisation in Srebrenica, was that the end of Srebrenica's problems, as you've described them? Or was the situation still difficult?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I myself was concerned, I can say that I was convinced it was the end and that it was the end of the war. But the situation remained exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were there any shelling incidents during demilitarisation that you recall?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the same way as in 1992, before demilitarisation but there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was your apartment ever damaged by any such incident?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just describe for us what happened to your apartment and what caused it.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the beginning of 1995. My husband and I went to bed, and there was a young man sleeping in our living-room, the two of us were sleeping in the bedroom, and at some point before dawn, I can tell you that it was before dawn because several hours had elapsed, and then it happened in the early morning, and we went to sleep and all of a sudden there was a loud bang and it was coming in the direction of my flat. And at that point, neither I myself nor my husband knew what it was but something exploded in our flat and when things calmed down a little bit, and then that is again followed by something horrible. My husband pushed me into the bathroom and covered me with a duvet and I almost broke the bathtub out of fear because I was looking for some kind of shelter because I felt as if every single bullet was meant for me. And it was a shell. I didn't know that it was a shell called Zolja, and we only found out the day after. My living room was destroyed. There was a lot of shrapnel shards, smoke, everything in the living-room had been damaged and destroyed, and, the day after, at least the three to four thousand people came by to see my flat, and every day I went to UNPROFOR and I asked the officials to come up and see what had happened but they never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, the damage you described to your apartment, you said, "I didn't know that it was a shell called Zolja," you found out the day after. Was this damage caused by a single shell or by more than one shell, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: At first, they launched that Zolja shell and then the attack went on for about 15 minutes. I thought that they were aiming at the hospital because the hospital is just below our building but it was probably too low and then they used machine guns. They were not even 50 metres away as the crow flies, I mean the Serbs that came down, and then they were firing machine-guns at my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware of any other shelling incidents which occurred during the demilitarisation period?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: It was in front of the school, primary and the secondary school, where there were quite a few refugees that were housed there, and we were a little bit more relaxed because we felt that the UNPROFOR people, the European monitors were there so we relaxed a little bit and men went out to play soccer. And of course I also felt the desire to relax a little bit and to watch the game because we had had enough of war and shooting already and then all of a sudden, two shells landed there, and a woman who was sitting next to me, I didn't know her, she just uttered the words, "My sons." And those two shells killed in excess of 70 people, at least that's what they said, and there were about 200 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know if there was an investigation by the local authorities into this incident?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: What local authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Jones. I take it that you'll start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness has to sign the map before we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please give the witness Exhibit D726. And could she please affix her signature at top, right-hand corner, please. You will start your cross-examination tomorrow, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And also if Your Honour could just advise the witness not to speak to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I will that. And you will finish tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say one thing, Your Honour? We notified a -- an exhibit list and I think generally you will have noticed we use the exhibits normally. This has been a rather extraordinary testimony in the sense that I haven't had the time really to use the exhibits, and I just want to say that it's generally if we notify the exhibits we are going to use them and it's just exceptionally today that I decided during the course of examination-in-chief not to use the exhibits. I apologise for any inconvenience to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. She's done it. Can I just -- let me see if I can see it from -- I need you to focus -- move it in a way that I can see the signature or bring the document here straight away. She hasn't signed it yet? Okay, could you please, Madam, could you please sign that map in the top right-hand corner, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So look at me, please, Madam Kolenovic. We are stopping here for today, also because Mr. Jones has finished with his examination-in-chief. Now, I'd like you to go back to your hotel and relax, try to unwind a little bit, because this has been obviously, evidently stressful. Tomorrow you are going to be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: she would finish tomorrow and she will certainly finish tomorrow. After that, you will be free to go back home. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stand adjourned to tomorrow. And it's a different courtroom if I remember well tomorrow. Courtroom III, Courtroom III, 9.00 in the morning. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, 1 September 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
